title: Ukraine's Largest Drone Manufacturer: Nearly 100,000 a Month, AI Interception Is Just the First Step
dek: Ukrainian drone maker General Cherry produces nearly 100,000 drones a month, including interceptors that down Russian Shaheds costing over $50,000 at a cost of about $2,000 each. AI guidance is already combat-proven, but full autonomy remains distant.
why: This episode is a rare first-hand account from a leading Ukrainian drone manufacturer about the real shape of battlefield drones, their costs, and the boundaries of AI application. It is information-dense and directly valuable for understanding modern warfare and the drone industry.
who: Founders, investors, and engineers focused on modern warfare, the drone industry, and military AI applications.
skip: The company introduction at the beginning can be skipped; go straight to the middle and later sections on AI and costs.

points.h: Nearly 100,000 a month, and capacity is still expanding
points.body: General Cherry was founded in 2023 and initially produced only about 10 drones a month. Today its monthly output reaches about 100,000 (the exact number is confidential). The company has partnered with more than 110 military brigades, and the best units consume over 5,000 drones a month. Capacity is still rising because battlefield consumption is enormous—drones have become consumables.

points.h: Ukraine has hundreds of drone companies, but only 10-15 are top-tier
points.body: The number of drone companies in Ukraine may be as high as 2,000, but the vast majority are garage-style workshops. Only 10 to 15 large companies can truly produce 1,000 to 10,000 drones a month, and General Cherry claims to be among the top five. This fragmented yet massive industrial ecosystem is the foundation of Ukraine's rapid innovation, but it also means fierce competition.

points.h: AI models are self-developed, co-created deeply with the military
points.body: General Cherry's AI guidance system is entirely self-developed. It has a strong R&D department and works closely with different military units on the front lines. They get battlefield feedback daily through mobile teams and iterate products quickly. This closed loop of "R&D—combat—feedback" allows Ukrainian drone technology to adapt rapidly to battlefield changes rather than relying on external procurement.

points.h: The rocket-shaped FPV originated with Red Bull, not Ukraine
points.body: This rocket-shaped FPV drone is not a Ukrainian invention. It was first used by Red Bull in 2021 or 2022 for sporting events. Ukrainian companies discovered that this shape can achieve higher speeds than ordinary quadcopters, so they adopted and optimized it. This reflects the rapid learning and pragmatism of Ukraine's drone industry—not pursuing originality, only effectiveness.

points.h: A $2,000 interceptor drone against a $50,000 Shahed
points.body: General Cherry's interceptor drones (such as Bullet) cost about $2,000 but can shoot down Russian Shahed drones that cost $50,000 to $100,000. This asymmetric cost exchange is Ukraine's key strategy for countering Russia's "saturation attacks"—using cheap drones to exhaust the enemy's expensive assets while avoiding the waste of expensive Western air-defense missiles.

points.h: Interceptors have confirmed over 5,000 Russian drones downed
points.body: Since production began in February 2025, General Cherry's tactical interceptor drone (General Trajectory Air) has confirmed shooting down more than 5,000 Russian drones. In December alone, it downed over 1,000 Russian "Moniya" drones. The model that intercepts Shaheds also entered mass production in December 2025, with confirmed kills approaching 1,000. These numbers show that interceptor drones have become an important force in battlefield air defense.

points.h: AI runs on the device, not in the cloud
points.body: General Cherry's AI guidance model runs on the drone's local camera chip, not in the cloud. After the operator detects a target via radar and launches the drone, the AI automatically identifies and locks onto the target without human intervention. This edge-AI design avoids battlefield communication delays and interference, which is key to making it viable in combat.

points.h: Fully autonomous weapons are a terrifying future, but AI is already inevitable
points.body: Marko admits that if drones become fully autonomous, it would be terrifying—killing would no longer require another person, only a robot or a drone. Currently they only use semi-autonomous AI on interceptor drones, because adding AI to ordinary FPVs significantly raises costs, and it is better to buy several more without AI. But he predicts AI technology will spread rapidly and prices will fall, making future battlefields even more brutal.
